title: Dedicated Capacity — Commitment & Procurement Negotiation Notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick, negotiable playbook for enterprise deals that want dedicated GPU capacity. Focus: procurement-ready language emphasizing SLAs, tenant isolation, predictable throughput, billing/commitment flexibility, and legal hooks buyers ask for. This is a working set — use as baseline for AE decks and procurement responses.

Background/context:
- We see larger deals moving from hosted API to Dedicated as soon as sustained QPS/latency predictability or regulatory isolation needs arise. Procurement teams ask for SLA language, isolation guarantees, and predictable unit economics.
- Common buyer archetypes:
  - Regulated enterprise (finance, healthcare) — needs VPC/private control plane, audit logs, KMS integration.
  - Platform/infra teams — care about throughput predictability, autoscale behavior, and noisy-neighbor isolation.
  - Product teams at scale — want cost-per-req predictability and rollback/fallback guarantees.

Key messaging pillars (short lines for slide headers / email intros):
- "Guaranteed throughput, predictable economics"
- "Isolation by design — capacity that behaves like your private fleet"
- "SLA-backed latency & availability so your product stays online"
- "Flexible commitment options to match procurement cycles"

Procurement-ready talking points (expandable):
1) SLA summary (what to surface to procurement buyer):
   - Uptime commitment: 99.9% monthly for primary pools (define maintenance windows and scheduled downtime notice period).
   - P99 latency target for standard models under committed throughput. Define model class buckets (small/medium/large) in annex.
   - Remedies: Service credits up to X% of monthly committed spend for unmet SLA tiers.
   - Measurement: Metrics published via Console (per-route latency, token throughput) + monthly SLA report with underlying raw telemetry available under NDA.

2) Isolation & multi-tenancy guarantees:
   - Dedicated GPU pools logically and physically isolated from other customers’ workloads in the same region.
   - Network isolation: optional VPC peering or private networking; no public egress for model KV cache traffic unless enabled.
   - Data handling: customer data no persisted to shared caches; KV caches may be pinned to pool and encrypted with customer-provided KMS (optional).
   - Attestation: SOC2/ISO artifacts available; optional on-prem package for air-gapped environments.

3) Predictable throughput & performance commitments:
   - Committed throughput defined as token-rate / concurrent-requests baseline with burst allowance. Specified in contract as "Committed QPS" or "Committed tokens/min".
   - Autoscaling behavior: configured to scale within committed pool with X% buffer for sustained spikes; bursts beyond buffer billed at overage rate or handled via paid burst capacity.
   - Fallback policy: automatic fallback to pinned model variant (quantized/replica) with documented quality delta if primary pool unable to serve; customer retains control of fallback rules.

4) Commercial/commitment options to propose:
   - Minimum term: 12 / 24 / 36 month options with stepped discounts.
   - Upfront vs monthly billing: tiered discounts for annual/NMP-like prepayments.
   - True-up cadence: quarterly usage true-up with clear overage price bands; options for locked unit pricing with defined ramp schedule.
   - Capacity credits: unused committed throughput may be banked for X quarters or converted to API credits for cross-product use.

5) Legal & compliance hooks commonly requested (quick responses):
   - Data residency: we can commit to region-bound serving and restrict backups.
   - Audit logging: 90/180/365 day retention options; exportable log package for audits.
   - Subprocessor list and right to audit under NDA.
   - Security controls: KMS/HSM integration, RBAC, SCIM provisioning, SSO.

Competitive notes (how to frame vs competitors):
- Versus public cloud managed endpoints: emphasize model-aware optimizations, cost-per-token control levers (batching, KV cache), and lower tail latency on long-context models. Public clouds often lack model-specialized kernels and batching policies.
- Versus self-hosted inference vendors: emphasize developer UX + turnkey observability + SLA + options for private deployments. Self-hosting gives control but pushes operational burden and unpredictable unit economics.
- Versus other LLM platform vendors: call out our fallback policies, per-route tracing and token-level cost breakdowns as procurement-visible differentiators.

Common procurement objections + suggested responses:
- "We need total control — we want on-prem only."
  - Response: We offer a Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) option; highlight support packages, transfer plan, and migration SLA. Start with Dedicated for quick time-to-value and move to Private on agreed timeline.
- "What if our usage spikes massively?"
  - Response: Dual-path: committed pool with burst buffer plus reserved burst capacity purchase; clearly documented auto-burst policy and throttling thresholds; can negotiate ratchet terms and surge credits.
- "How do we prove performance?"
  - Response: Provide a pre-sales bench: synthetic workload run on proposed pool config, runbook of test, and sample P99 metrics; include a short pilot with defined success criteria.

AE playbook (short steps for closing):
1) Qualification call — capture model classes, concurrency needs, retention/regulatory requirements, and procurement timeline.
2) Propose commitment tier + pilot (4–6 weeks) with clear acceptance criteria tied to latency & throughput.
3) Present procurement slide pack (SLA summary, isolation bullets, fallback behavior, pricing bands, legal hooks).
4) Run procurement security questionnaire (send SOC artifacts, sample contract addenda).
5) Negotiate term/true-up and finalize SOW + onboarding milestones.

Pilot success criteria template (to include in SOW):
- Achieve committed throughput X tokens/min with P99 latency <= Y ms for 95% of runs.
- Demonstrate fallback behavior does not increase error rate by >Z%.
- Deliver observability dashboard with route-level cost breakdown and traceability.

Open questions / decisions we need from product/infra/legal: (use these as quick asks in the deal cycle)
- Define standard SLA credit table (percent credits per minute/hour of downtime) and which incidents are excluded.
- Formalize pool isolation language (wording that legal is comfortable with while still being attractive to buyers).
- Default true-up cadence and banked credit policy (how many quarters credits are valid).

Appendix: short boilerplate snippets AEs can copy into proposals
- Isolation snippet: "Redwood will allocate a dedicated GPU pool for Customer, logically and physically partitioned from other customers in the region. Customer workloads will not share KV caches with non-customer workloads unless explicitly configured by the Customer."
- SLA synopsis: "Redwood commits to 99.9% availability for Dedicated pools. P99 latency targets for committed throughput tiers are specified in the annex; service credits will be applied per the SLA schedule for missed targets."

Notes/to-dos (informal):
- Miguel: draft SLA credit table and annex model size tiers.
- Priya: prepare two slide templates (short and expanded procurement pack).
- Ben: coordinate quick pre-sales bench run template and sample telemetry export.
- Follow up with Legal to set guardrails on isolation language by EOD next week.

End — this is intentionally short/portable — adapt for customer-facing collateral as we finalize legal wording.
